chunks: He whom sin overpowers is not victorious, and he who secures victory by evil is (in fact) vanquished.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between worldly victory and true spiritual success in Shia ethics?
ai.summary: In this maxim from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) employs a paradoxical rhetorical structure to redefine victory (zafar) not by external success but by internal moral integrity. This concept aligns with the Shia scholarly emphasis on the 'hidden defeat' of the righteous who may appear to lose worldly battles but retain spiritual supremacy, contrasting with the 'illusory triumph' of those consumed by sin. The statement serves as a critical ethical framework for evaluating leadership and personal conduct, asserting that the dominant force of evil ultimately enslaves the victor.

en.sayed-ali-raza: 327. Amīr al-mu’minīn, peace be upon him, said:
He whom sin overpowers is not victorious, and he who secures victory by evil is (in fact) vanquished.
